meta.title: Otter.ai Founder on the Future of AI Meetings | The Next Endeavor 2026
meta.thread_line: 5 threads · in-house speech tech · conversational knowledge engine · seat to usage pricing · privacy and behavior · coaching and the future of meetings

snapshot: Sam Liang founded Otter in 2016 because he could search Gmail for anything but not what was said in a meeting three hours earlier.
Otter built its own speech recognition and speaker identification; it says Zoom licensed that technology from 2017 to 2023 and that it still has the better technology.
The pitch is a **conversational knowledge engine**: capture meetings, build a knowledge graph of people, projects and customers, then act (for example send a Slack message) so people stop typing.
Otter is at **$100M ARR**; Liang says its addressable market is well above the $100B CRM-sized figure because every team holds meetings.
Pricing will likely move from per-seat to usage-based, as agents already do for Anthropic.
Recording changes behavior at first but people will take it for granted; enterprises need access control, redaction and off-the-record modes.
Financial firms are an unexpectedly strong customer vertical, using Otter for training and live coaching.

themes.title: Why Otter built its own speech stack, and what Zoom's licensing says about it
themes.lead: Liang bet that no off-the-shelf model handled long multi-speaker conversations, so Otter built transcription and speaker identification itself.
bullets: Liang led Google's mobile map location platform from 2006 to 2010, then built a mobile startup that was acquired before founding Otter with a co-founder ten years ago.
The spark: Gmail and search let him find anything, but he couldn't search something he heard three hours ago; he says he has a bad memory.
In 2016 Google Voice, Siri and Alexa weren't trained for long multi-speaker conversations, so Otter tested everything and built its own recognition.
All Otter transcription and speaker identification is in-house, with no third-party API, which he says makes it highly accurate and fast.
Speaker attribution matters: he says Google Meet and Zoom can't separate multiple people in one room, and Otter has worked on it for ten years.
Zoom licensed Otter's technology for transcripts between 2017 and 2023; Liang says Zoom stopped after its IPO but that Otter still has better technology.
Copycats now exist: Google and Zoom embed their own transcription and summaries, yet Liang says Otter is still growing rapidly.
themes.watch: Liang is the founder describing his company's own technical lead and the Zoom history; the host says his own meetings run through Otter and a wearable recorder.

themes.title: From transcripts to a knowledge graph that acts on your behalf
themes.lead: Voice is the most overlooked source of business knowledge, and Otter wants it to feed actions so nobody types into a CRM again.
bullets: Managers can spend 70-80% of their time in meetings, which is where most business intelligence is generated and then lost.
Three stages: capture as many meetings as possible (most are still not captured), understand the content, then act.
The knowledge graph links entities such as people, projects and customers, and learns who needs to collaborate with whom.
Action example: say 'I need to tell Simon' and the engine sends the Slack message; it can also notify you when a colleague's change affects your work.
Customers own their data; Otter calls it an engine because it takes action, not just stores knowledge.
Voice-first: Liang says he just hired someone who codes entirely by voice, and he expects most people won't need to type eventually.
The host cites psychology studies that people are happiest when speaking and says the keyboard is not a natural interface.

quote.text: Eventually most people don't need to type anymore.

themes.title: From per-seat to usage pricing, and a TAM bigger than CRM
themes.lead: The host asks whether note-taking becomes a free embedded feature or a hundreds-of-billions product; Liang says the business model will evolve toward usage.
bullets: Otter is at $100M ARR; its slide claims a $100B category, which Liang calls an underestimate because CRM covers only sales while every team holds meetings.
The host's CRM analogy: CRM could have been a $50 product but Siebel and Salesforce charged $10,000 a seat by proving productivity gains; Otter faces the same fork.
Liang says most SaaS uses seat pricing but more products are moving to usage-based pricing, and he cites Anthropic's agent products making money that way.
He expects Otter to adopt usage-based pricing, with outputs like an automatic product requirements document written from a one-hour brainstorm.
Verticals: software companies are core customers; finance is a surprisingly strong second, despite being slow to adopt AI.
themes.watch: Liang is also selling a company whose valuation depends on this TAM argument.

themes.title: Recording everything: behavior change, redaction and off-the-record controls
themes.lead: Liang expects people to take constant recording for granted, but enterprises need exceptions and tight access control.
bullets: The host says people act differently when recorded; Liang agrees it changes behavior today but expects people to eventually assume everything is captured.
Exceptions: one-on-ones, HR, legal and financial matters need access control or no capture.
Otter is building a redaction mode and an off-the-record option to remove sensitive content; Liang says it should be good but is still being worked on.
Customer meetings are encrypted and Otter can't see them, so he can't tell the host the most outrageous thing it has transcribed.
Always-on glasses and pendants with video and audio are coming, but nobody in the Silicon Valley room was wearing them and many people avoid it.
themes.watch: The redaction and off-the-record features are described as still in progress, so the trust question stays open.

themes.title: Live coaching, self-grading and whether meetings survive AI
themes.lead: Otter already coaches in real time and Liang grades his own performance with it, while he guesses meetings may fade in 5-10 years.
bullets: Live coaching: during a Zoom or Meet call with a customer the AI listens and feeds answers you can read back when you can't answer a question.
Self-grading: after customer meetings Liang asks AI whether he asked the right questions, caught cues or talked too much; he thinks it applies to personal life too.
A finance customer said training a new associate takes almost a year; they now use Otter to speed it up through simulated conversations scored in real time.
Liang's personal fantasy is capturing all of his life, voice included, as a coach and assistant, but the company is focused on the team use case.
The host asks whether AI could tell a CEO when they're wrong; Liang says an AI is easier to take than a person.
Debate raised by the host: at MIT most hold that AI amplifies a few people in a room (camp A), at Stanford more say AI will originate ideas (camp B), and nobody predicts it well.
Liang's ideal: at the end of a meeting, the AI says all action items are already finished; meetings may eventually not be needed in 5 or 10 years.

quote.text: If you tell the CEO they're wrong, they're offended. But if AI tells them, they're probably okay. What do you do with AI? You cannot fire them.

takeaways.title: Capture the voice channel, since most business knowledge is spoken and never written down.
Build a knowledge graph of people, projects and customers on top of transcripts to enable actions.
Plan the move from per-seat to usage-based pricing if your product does work for the user.
Ship access control, redaction and off-the-record modes before pushing always-on capture.
Test live coaching and post-call self-grading for customer-facing teams, as finance firms are doing.

hot_takes.take: Eventually most people don't need to type anymore.
If you tell the CEO they're wrong, they're offended. But if AI tells them, they're probably okay.
hot_takes.why: Argues AI can deliver unwelcome feedback better.

hot_takes.take: The total addressable market will be actually way bigger than 100 billion.
hot_takes.why: Calls his own $100B TAM an underestimate.

hot_takes.take: Eventually maybe you don't need to meet anymore because AI will do everything.
hot_takes.why: Predicts meetings could disappear within 5-10 years.

claims.claim: Meetings may become unnecessary as AI does the work, though it will still take some years.
Otter moves to usage-based pricing as products shift from per-seat models.

relations.note: Zoom licensed its transcription technology 2017-2023; Liang says it stopped after Zoom's IPO

other_news.title: Sources referenced: a MIT versus Stanford debate about whether LLMs only interpolate (relayed by the host), psychology studies on happiness while speaking, and Anthropic's usage-based agent products.
Liang runs marathons and wears two watches to track health metrics; he wants emotional and intellectual data (voice) captured as well.
Joke use case: recording wedding promises with Otter and reviewing how many were fulfilled.
